responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

This is a special themed issue on the work of child psychotherapists in schools. It begins with two scholarly, informative and fascinating historical articles on the application of psychoanalytic ideas to education in the early part of the 20th century, and the involvement of two major psychoanalytic figures from the period. Each of these articles discusses an experimental school set up and organised on the basis of psychoanalytic principles and ideas. Both these thoroughly researched articles, rich in historical detail, vividly bring to life the people involved and the ideas underlying their practice. These are followed by a range of articles covering a variety of themes and issues linked to the work of contemporary psychoanalytic child psychotherapists in schools. This edition is a testimony to the longstanding, pioneering and creative tradition of applying psychoanalytic thinking in the field of education.

The opening article, ‘Susan Isaacs and the Malting House School’, is an exemplary guest contribution by Professor Philip Graham, Emeritus Professor of Child Psychiatry at the Institute of Child Health, London. Professor Graham's erudite and captivating article is a comprehensive account of the experimental Malting House School open from 1924–1929 and run by Susan Isaacs, who later became a close associate of Melanie Klein. The article briefly sets the historical context of the progressive school movement in England, and then gives an absorbing description of the setting up, the philosophy, the running and the organisation of the school, concluding with an evaluation of the influence of the school and of Susan Isaacs on the promotion of the theory and practice of child centred education. For those interested in reading further on this subject, a fuller account of the Malting House School and of the life of Susan Isaacs is available in a forthcoming book by Professor Graham, Susan Isaacs: Freeing the Minds of Children (in press, Karnac).

The following article by Nick Midgley, ‘The “Matchbox School” (1927–1932): Anna Freud and the idea of a “psychoanalytically-informed education”’ complements the previous one. Midgley's in-depth, extensive and wide-ranging paper begins by describing the debates around pedagogy in the wider European context at that time. The influence of two key figures on Anna Freud's thinking about psychoanalysis and education is then discussed. The teaching methods of the school, the members of staff, the student group, ongoing debates about the values and principles on which the school was organised and run, as well as perceptions of the school in the wider psychoanalytic and educational communities are all detailed and discussed. Like the previous article, there is an evaluation of the contribution of the school – and in this case of Anna Freud – both in relation to the application of psychoanalytic thinking to the practice and theory of education, and to the individual pupils who attended the school.

Exploring the therapeutic process

[All abstracts are reproduced with the permission of the publishers.]

Can research influence clinical practice?

Juan Pablo Jimenez

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, June 2007, Volume 88 (3): 661–79.

After briefly reviewing the unfavourable reception accorded empirical research by parts of the psychoanalytic community, as well as some of the benefits to clinical practice of analysts being involved in research activities, the author examines whether the findings of process and outcome research in psychotherapy and psychoanalysis can help identify the most appropriate forms of intervention for producing therapeutic change, given the specific condition of the patient and the relationship that the individual establishes with the analyst. He argues that research findings can influence clinical practice on various levels and in different areas, and goes on to examine a number of related issues: the specificity of therapeutic interventions versus the relevance of common curative factors; the dyadic conception of technique and ways of understanding the therapeutic action of the treatment alliance; and the strategic or heuristic conception in psychoanalytic therapy. Finally, the author presents clinical material with the aim of illustrating how the knowledge acquired through research can be applied to psychoanalytic treatment.

The clinical concept of analytic process: a conceptual investigation

Manuel Pires Dos Santos, Maria Lúcia Tiellet Nunes & Lúcia Freitas Ceitlin

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, April 2006, Volume 87 (2): 403–22.

The authors discuss the term ‘analytic process’, confirming the variability of the meanings ascribed to it.

Creating New Families: Therapeutic Approaches to Fostering, Adoption and Kinship Care

Jenny Kenrick, Caroline Lindsey and Lorraine Tollemarche (eds)

London: Karnac, 2006

312 pp., £18.99

This timely and comprehensive book addresses the complex needs of children who are fostered, adopted or looked after by kinship carers. Most permanent alternative family placements follow years of very difficult experiences for children in birth families, and the majority of adoptions nowadays are of older children. As society moves through massive turbulence and change, the numbers of Looked After Children continue to rise (an increase of 3% between 2001 and 2005); the numbers of children in family placements are, however, growing more rapidly and a 9% increase is seen in those fostered in that same period, while 38% more children were adopted. All children are growing up in the fluid and often unstable social context of the modern world, many in complex and fragile family structures, thus often the complexity of children's needs is greater.

The children who are at the heart of this book may go through multiple placements and/or wait a long time to be permanently placed. They will bring with them complex conscious memories of earlier families, accompanied by correspondingly complex internal worlds, alongside of and in the light of which, new families must take shape. The book offers a careful, vibrant and accessible account of the intricate processes of making sense of the experiences of children who are unable to remain with their families of origin, and of the profound and often unpredictable endeavour that is the creation of a new family. The book explores and demonstrates the demands as well as the potential with which these new opportunities face each participant child, parent and professional as the task of integrating old and new within child, family and network unfolds.

The title of the book and indeed the name of the specialist, multidisciplinary team which has contributed to it – The Fostering, Adoption, and Kinship Care team at the Tavistock Clinic – reflect the considerable shift over the past 10 years or so in thinking about children in transition. Changing ideas about the kinds of work and the timing of therapeutic interventions with children in transition are lucidly demonstrated and supported by evidence of developments in theory and in practice which is carefully thought through and increasingly researched.

[[RunningHead]]

Say hello to the scream extractor: working with an autistic child with psychotic mechanisms

Lesley Maroni

Lesley Maroni

Lesley Maroni  

Psychic retreat, fragmentation, fusion, omnipotence, psychic bisexuality, attacks on linking

Abstract

This paper describes the first two years of intensive psychotherapy with a six-year-old boy diagnosed with autism. I explore the many ways in which he retreated from reality, most frequently by taking refuge inside the maternal body or flying off into an imaginary space world. He fragmented his identity and that of his objects by using the discourse of fictional characters. Everything was externalised; there was little transmutation of material available for thought. I consider his dilemma – the wish to fuse with the object and the fear of being engulfed; the omnipotent denial of the need for an object and of the parental relationship, leading to an inability to make links. The paper discusses working with a child who experienced any ‘paternal’ firmness as persecuting and destructive. The softer, receptive maternal mind of the therapist was more easily tolerated. He gradually began to internalise a more benign combined object, as he became more able to bear separateness from the other.

[[RunningHead]]

Clinical Commentary

Clinical material

Background

Finn is a fostered boy aged eight, seen three times a week for psychotherapy. He and an older sibling were removed from his parents when Finn was aged five, and placed with the current foster carers. The placement has periodically been jeopardised by his chaotic and destructive behaviour, which includes instances of harming a neighbour's pets. In Finn's home of origin, he and five older siblings formed a feral gang whose activities went unmonitored by his parents, often absent. In his first five years, he was exposed to the sadism and drug taking of his eldest brother and friends. He was physically neglected and often went hungry, since he was dependent on older siblings to procure him something to eat. He was referred because of his sadism towards animals, his destructive behaviour and a relentless preoccupation with food. He has intermittent contact with his parents, which he anticipates with both excitement and distress.

Finn's foster mother is seen every two weeks by a social worker colleague, but she continues to find it hard to put herself in his shoes, or to see that there is a relationship between his current behaviour and his early history. There are also regular and productive network meetings involving social workers and teachers, which have played a role in making his placement more stable. Finn attends an EBD school, where there is intermittent concern about his distractibility and disruptive behaviour. He has friends, but tends to become a ringleader and involves them in his comic misdemeanours. Aside from this, he is a bright, imaginative child who is reading and writing well for his age.

In his sessions, Finn is endearing, funny and affectionate, but can become extremely chaotic, physically aggressive and destructive when he is anxious. Shifts of mood take place with disconcerting rapidity and unpredictability, and in the countertransference I experience these transformations as both frightening and hurtful. Early sessions were spent trying to manage his behaviour as he ran about the clinic, kicked and pinched me, and tried to flood the room and damage its furnishings with scissors. He has, however, rapidly made use of me as an adult who will tolerate, verbalise and try to understand his feelings. He was initially bemused that I would allow myself to be involved in his games, and now often uses me to play out, in the realm of pretend, the terror and deprivation of his early environment.

Notes for a dialogue between psychoanalysis and neuroscience

Franco Scalzone

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, October 2005, Volume 86 (5): 1405–23.

The author postulates that the dialogue between psychoanalysis and neuroscience is based on the assumption that both deal with virtual structures. They are two facets of the same noumenal reality, but with different phenomenal realities, and it is possible to use metapsychology as a lingua franca to develop communication between the two fields. In the second part of the paper, the author reflects on the results of recent neurophysiological research which seem to offer to psychoanalysis possibilities for finding an anatomical physiological correlate of some well-known psychic phenomena and mechanisms, such as imitation, introjection, identification, empathy, identity, mother–child communication, learning, social communication and the analyst–patient relationship. Particular neurons, called mirror neurons, have been located in the F5 area of baboons' brains. They are also present in man's brain within Broca's area. These neurons activate our motor system during both the performance of actions and the observation of actions performed by others giving rise to an automatic response, a sort of simulation or, rather, imitation, as the process is not intentional, but automatic and unaware, that is, unconscious.

The case against neuropsychoanalysis: on fallacies underlying psychoanalysis' latest scientific trend and its negative impact on psychoanalytic discourse

Rachel Blass & Zvi Carmeli

The International Journal of Psychoanalysis, February 2007, Volume 88 (1): 19–40.

The authors offer a critical examination of the claims of the proponents of the growing neuropsychoanalytic trend, that neuroscientific findings are relevant and important for the development and justification of psychoanalytic theory and practice.

‘Pussy Cat, Pussy Cat, Where have you been?’An account of intensive psychotherapy with a seven-year-old boy in a special school

Kate Robertson

Kate Robertson

Kate Robertson  

Developmental delay, adaptations to psychotherapy, rhythm, inside, outside, music therapy

Abstract

This paper gives an account of the developments in the intensive psychotherapy of a seven-year-old boy with global development delay. It also describes the adaptations to technique and the changes in the setting that were required to support the work, which was undertaken in a special school. The importance of the regularity of sessions in helping to establish object constancy; physical and mental boundaries in relation to me/not me; inside and outside is also explored. A central theme of the paper is how close observation can inform the understanding of the emotional states of disabled children, particularly those with little language. The paper draws links between the early communications of mothers and infants and the therapeutic relationship, with reference to music therapy. It describes banging as a form of communication and traces the development of banging into more coherent nursery rhymes arguing that this development is an internalisation of the rhythm of the therapy and of the growing understanding between the child and therapist.

Clinical Commentary

Clinical material

Session 1

Mr and Mrs T came to the room followed by their son Max aged three and a half. The parents are in their mid-30s. Max was on the couch, playing with the toy animals while the parents each sat in an armchair. When asked what had brought them to the clinic the parents looked at one another as though not sure how to start or who should speak first and then Mr T looked at Mrs T and asked who will tell the story, Mrs T decided she would like to begin.

Mrs T firstly commented on how quickly they had been offered an appointment following her phone call to the clinic. She then, in a calm but strained manner, explained that the reason they wanted to talk with someone was because Max didn't sleep through the night. She explained that he had never really slept well and recently the sleep difficulties had become worse. She described how Max was able to fall asleep but on a bad night he woke up at about 1:00 a.m. and from then on until morning she has to attend to Max waking on an hourly basis. On a good night, she will only have to go in to him three or four times. She said that the sleepless nights were becoming increasingly difficult and were now impacting on their relationship and they needed some help. Mr T confirmed everything his wife said.

When asked what thoughts the parents had about what may be unsettling Max, Mrs T became quite anxious and immediately linked his difficulties to her attempts to wean him from the bottle. She questioned whether she was doing the right thing, saying she had read numerous books, naming one in particular. She said she had tried several techniques to wean him but it had always been difficult, as Max had not found any substitutes like his thumb or a blanket to soothe himself. Again, in quite an anxious way she questioned whether what she was doing was right.

She then described how both Mr and Mrs T, with Max, had recently made an agreement that Max could have a bottle at night when he falls asleep and one in the morning in bed with mum and dad. However, Max still woke throughout the night wanting the bottle.

Psychoanalytic psychotherapy assessment in a child and adolescent mental health setting: an exploratory study

Cecile Petit & Nick Midgley

Clinical Child Psychology and Psychiatry, January 2008, Volume 13 (1): 139–55

Undertaking assessment is a significant component of a Child Psychotherapist's work within Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS), yet as an activity it has been relatively neglected in the research literature. This study made use of a small-scale, qualitative design to explore the nature and function of psychoanalytic assessment work within a single CAMHS team. After an initial audit of child psychotherapy assessment work, in-depth interviews with 5 Child and Adolescent Psychotherapists, exploring the nature of assessment work, were analysed using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA). Results suggested that assessment is a major part of the Child Psychotherapist's work, although there are different types of assessment done in different contexts. Among the participants there was a certain shared understanding of the psychoanalytic approach to assessment, although with significant differences in regard to process, technique (e.g. use of interpretation, the role of countertransference) and the reporting of assessments. The analysis also suggested tensions between the role of the assessor as an ‘expert’ and as a ‘therapist’.

Author biographies

Tessa Baradon came from the field of Public Health to child psychoanalysis and psychotherapy. She has worked in the public and private sectors, and has been responsible for the planning and provision of services for parents and infants in the National Health Service and initiated and developed the Parent Infant Project at The Anna Freud Centre. She is a practicing child therapist and supervisor, and writes and lectures on child psychoanalysis and parent infant psychotherapy. She is Member of the Association of Child Psychotherapists and the Association of Child Psychoanalysis, Inc.

Kirsten Bland worked as a research psychologist at The Anna Freud Centre. She carried out the interviews and assessments with the mothers and babies in this study. She has also worked on several other parent–infant outreach studies. She is currently completing her training in Clinical Psychology at the University of Edinburgh.

Diana Cant is a consultant child and adolescent psychotherapist with Childhood First (formerly the Peper Harow Foundation) and in private practice. She also acts as consultant to the staff teams at a number of CAMHS clinics in Kent. She has worked in several therapeutic communities, including 10 years at the Caldecott Community, and has a particular interest in residential work with severely damaged children. The Emotional Experience of Adoption

The Emotional Experience of Adoption

Debbie Hindle and Graham Shulman (eds)

Routledge: Abingdon and New York, 2008

280 pp., £23.99

Reading this book is in itself an emotional experience, and one that is potentially life-changing for those whose life has been touched by adoption, whether personally or as a professional.

The book focuses, as it says in the title, on the many and complex emotions that are stirred by adoption in the children being adopted, in those adopting them, and by the professionals in the surrounding network. Several of the contributors acknowledge in their biographies that they are the parents of adopted children, and the sense of felt experience is palpable in the book.

In their introduction, Debbie Hindle and Graham Shulman set out their understanding of the complexity of the emotional task of adoption:

It is a field in which the diverse realms of individual experience and society interact. It spans the inner and outer worlds in particularly complicated ways. It involves the internal worlds of the birth family and adoptive child and family; the themes of parental sexuality, procreation or infertility; the professional networks around looked-after children and around adoption and adoptive families; the law and the legal system; social and cultural values and beliefs; ideology; and even myth. As a psychological field, adoption thus involves a distinctive constellation of emotional forces. (p. 1)

The book focuses on this complex field, and aims ‘to promote interest in, and curiosity about, the potential applications of a psychoanalytic perspective to the adoption process, and its relevance to the experience of adoption, amongst a wider audience than those who might access articles in professional journals’ (p. 3). The aim of the book is to think and reflect, not to advocate a particular way of working, but to raise awareness of the many dimensions of the emotions involved in adoption which need to be held in mind when working in this field.

Abstract

This paper describes the application of child psychotherapy, its theory and practice, in a Pupil Referral Unit (PRU). It examines the importance of a flexible approach to outreach work and the implementation of interventions that take into consideration both the internal and the external world of the adolescent. Furthermore, the process of development of a psychodynamic group with PRU students is described and illustrated. Additionally, it explores the importance of developing psychodynamic models of working with allied professionals in supervision and collaborative efforts in general. The paper explores the usefulness of the concept of mentalisation when working in the context of schools as well as the need to develop an accessible psychodynamic language that enables multidisciplinary collaboration. Overall, this paper reflects on the importance of holding in mind the challenge of balancing the needs of the external and the internal world, which becomes very evident in the process of outreach work.

Joining up with ‘not us’ staff to run adolescent groups in schools

Suzan Sayder

Suzan Sayder

Suzan Sayder  

Adolescent groups, school groups, applied child psychotherapy, group processes, emotional management

Abstract

The author describes the development of a model for working with staff members from non-psychoanalytic backgrounds to run therapeutic and therapy-like pupil groups in schools. She draws on her experience of co-facilitating groups at a London-based secondary school and uses examples from recent group work with Year 10 pupils (aged 14–15). Child psychotherapists who have shied away either from doing group work in general, or more specifically taking on group work in schools, may be encouraged to see that the underlying principles are essentially no different from those of individual therapy. Worrying and troublesome young people tend to have difficulties in their external relationships, often exhibited at school and contributing to their underachievement. Psychoanalytically informed groups such as the kind portrayed here can address this difficulty by offering a safe setting for interactions with other group participants and with the leaders to be observed, examined and challenged in the here and now. Attention is paid to primitive anxieties and the defences employed to keep them at bay, including the tendency to place individual needs before group needs when sense of self and sometimes survival itself are felt to be threatened. The aim is for participants to learn about themselves by sharing a group experience and, if successful, integrate some conflicting aspects of themselves. This model for doing group work demonstrates how child psychotherapists can make a unique and valuable contribution, provided the school environment is conducive and there is a member of staff who is open to learning a new way of working.

Philip Graham is Emeritus Professor of Child Psychiatry at the Institute of Child Health, London, where he was Dean from 1985 to 1990. From 1968 to 1994, he was consultant child psychiatrist at the Hospital for Sick Children, Great Ormond Street, London. He has a long-standing interest in education, having served on the Warnock Committee on Children with Special Educational Needs (1978). His most recent publications are Child Psychiatry: A Developmental Approach (joint author), 4th edition, 2007, OUP; Cognitive Behaviour Therapy for Children and Families, 2nd edition, 2005, CUP; and The End of Adolescence, 2004, OUP.

Becky Hall is currently in her final year of the Tavistock Child Psychotherapy Training and works at Parkside Clinic in West London. She was previously an assistant psychotherapist for TOPS, the Tavistock Outreach Programme in Schools, and before that she was working on a PhD in Literature at the University of York.

Emil Jackson is a consultant child and adolescent psychotherapist working at the Tavistock Clinic and Brent Centre for Young People. Alongside his clinical and teaching role, he has been actively involved in the development of outreach projects in educational settings and, in particular, in the development of work discussion groups for teachers, middle and senior managers. In addition to his clinical and consultancy work, he teaches on a number of courses at the Tavistock Clinic, including the professional doctorate in child psychotherapy and the masters programme in working with groups.

Norka T. Malberg is a child and adolescent psychotherapist. She obtained degrees in the USA in the areas of Clinical Psychology and Educational Psychology with a specialisation in working with children and families at risk from Harvard University. Prior to her arrival in London in 1999, she worked in Chile in private practice and developed initiatives to encourage the prevention of child sexual abuse. She was subsequently the school psychologist at the International School of Zurich where she attended lectures at the Jungian Institute. She trained as a child and adolescent psychotherapist at the Anna Freud Centre where she currently works focusing on the development of outreach initiatives and working with children in short-term and long-term psychoanalytic psychotherapy. She has a private practice in North London. She recently received her doctorate in child and adolescent psychotherapy from University College London for her development of a psychodynamic group in the context of the Renal Unit at Great Ormond Street Unit.

Tripartite therapy with older children: mutuality in the relationship of a parent–child attachment

Nancy Berlin

Nancy Berlin

Nancy Berlin  

Mother–child attachment, parent–child psychotherapy, tripartite psychotherapy, attachment therapy, attachment deficits

Abstract

This is the last of a series of three papers exploring the use with older children of tripartite psychotherapy – a technique of psychoanalytic psychotherapy of the parent–child relationship with both parent and child in the room together with the therapist. Tripartite psychotherapy merits more attention than it has received. It is a flexible, psychoanalytically oriented approach to parent–child relationship problems, particularly useful when the primary attachment has gone awry. A study is presented of a mother and her 12-year-old (adopted) daughter, who are embroiled in a hostile and rejecting relationship. The mutuality in this case illustrates the complexity in attachment relationships, and also how useful tripartite psychotherapy can be in working with attachment issues that often present as problems of the child alone.

Editorial

Graham Shulman and Viviane Green

Viviane Green

Viviane Green  

This is a general edition of the Journal, which reflects both the range of work undertaken by child psychotherapists and the variety of settings within which child psychotherapists work. Articles on looked after children remain a recurring theme in the Journal, reflecting the significant number of such children who enter into psychotherapy and the complexities involved in their development, particularly as, unfortunately, a number of them have repeated changes of caregivers or placements that break down, or else need to grow up in care. The looked after child is embedded in a network of professional carers and working agencies. In this edition, we are fortunate that two authors, Simon Cregeen and Marigemma Rocco-Briggs, address several of the complex issues involved in the network(s) around the children. Unsurprisingly, the children and adolescents mobilise powerful responses in the networks surrounding them as the issues they bring ricochet within the teams, setting up various dynamics. Quoting Britton, Cregeen reminds us that ‘when family breakdown has occurred, the child may or may not be homeless, but he is psychically unplaced’. A critical task for residential workers, as his article illustrates vividly, is to help the young person feel psychically placed. By extension, the consultant's role is to help recover the place of the child in the mind of the workers. Rocco-Briggs echoes this theme in taking up psychic displacement as the intolerable underlying feeling of no longer belonging to parents whose acts towards the child are too unbearable for the child to bring into, let alone keep in, mind. The powerful enactments are replayed at the institutional or team level, mobilising defences that militate against being understood and appropriately held in mind.

Simon Cregeen, in his article ‘Worker, groups and gangs: consultation to residential adolescent teams', reflects on his in-depth experience in acting as a consultant to the staff of children's homes. He underscores the complex internal object related trajectory of looked after children whose ‘internal parental objects and couplings … inevitably include those of abandoning, abusive and ambivalent parental figures’. These internal figures are projected and enacted at all levels, between the adolescents and their workers, through to the team and consultant. His article, with animated detail, subtly traces the moment-to-moment movement within consultations as the different states of mind are played out within the team. The countertransference pressures on the consultant make for absorbing reading, especially when we see how the author processes invitations to narcissistic gratification or ‘corruption’. New Beginnings–an experience-based programme addressing the attachment relationship between mothers and their babies in prisons

Tessa Baradon , Peter Fonagy , Kirsten Bland , Kata Lénárd and Michelle Sleed

Michelle Sleed

Michelle Sleed  

Attachment, mothers and babies, high-risk, prison Mother and Baby Units, early intervention, reflective functioning, intergenerational transmission

Abstract

Data about the quality of attachment between infants and parents in high-risk populations suggests that early intervention may be advantageous for positive developmental outcomes for the child. Mothers in prison represent a high-risk parenting population in terms of both attachment histories and economic and social risk factors. New Beginnings was constructed as a short term, experience-based programme for mothers and infants in the Mother and Baby Units of two UK women's prisons. It is based on the early intervention model developed at the Anna Freud Centre. The programme was piloted in 2004–5, with 27 participating dyads. This paper presents an overview of the pilot stage. Our aim is to introduce the thinking that went into the programme and to present initial observations concerning the effect of the programme. We describe the development of a framework for the programme and its preliminary evaluation using pre- and post-interview protocols concerning the mothers' thoughts and feelings about their babies. We used the Parent Development Interview, for both a qualitative analysis of the major themes in connection to child rearing and quantitative measures of reflective capacity in relation to the child on the part of mother-participants.

Beth Miller

Beth Miller

Beth Miller  

Autism, Asperger's syndrome, claustrum, adhesive identification, autistic terror, trans-generational issues

Abstract

This paper is an account of the intensive psychotherapy of a young girl on the autistic spectrum. It describes her confusing presentation and how this suggested a tendency to oscillate between mainly unintegrated states of mind. Important themes that emerged included the phantasy of inhabiting a claustrum; the use of adhesive identification to defend against the bodily felt terror of separation; and fear of damage to the maternal object. The paper also discusses the trans-generational aspects of her difficulties and considers how her therapy helped growth to take place.

Abstract

The ‘Matchbox School’ (1927–1932): Anna Freud and the idea of a ‘psychoanalytically informed education’*

Nick Midgley

Nick Midgley

Nick Midgley  

Psychoanalysis, progressive education, Anna Freud, the Matchbox School, project method, pedagogy

Abstract

Of all the applications of psychoanalysis to various fields, perhaps none has been as important – or as fraught – as the application of psychoanalytic insights to education. This paper re-constructs some of the early debates around psychoanalysis and pedagogy that Anna Freud engaged with during the 1920s in Vienna, when the whole question of what education should be became a central issue for politicians, pedagogues and psychoanalysts alike. The paper focuses on the period leading up to the creation of the so-called ‘Matchbox School’, operating under Anna Freud's guidance between 1927 and 1932, and describes the influence of pioneers such as Seigfried Bernfeld and August Aichhorn. Compared to her more well-known work at the Hampstead War Nurseries during the Second World War, Anna Freud's involvement with this earlier educational experiment is relatively neglected. Yet one can argue that this short-lived project not only laid the foundation for much of Anna Freud's later work; it also had some far-reaching consequences, both for psychoanalysis and for the practice of progressive education.

Affective association: an effective intervention in countering fragmentation and dissociation

Carolyn Hart

Carolyn Hart

Carolyn Hart  

Affect attunement, dissociation, mentalisation, mirror neurons, neuroscience, projective identification, tremor

Abstract

This paper is concerned with the processes, both psychoanalytic and neuroscientific, involved in the undoing of dissociation in a 3-year-old, who was seen weekly over a nine month period. A neuroscientific and psychoanalytic developmental framework is used to follow a sequence of phenomena that emerged over the duration of relatively brief once weekly psychotherapy. Splintered aspects of the personality are shown to co-exist using different but related primitive defences, namely: dissociation, projective identification and somatic tremor. Clinical material of this traumatised child is used to illustrate the struggle to regulate changing affective states and their manifestations and to suggest a developmental progression occurring during the psychotherapy. Speculatively it is suggested that whilst mirror neurons would have been present from birth, the process of dissociation inhibited their functioning. One of the outcomes of therapy was to recruit mirror neurons in the service of developing processes of identification and empathy. Only then could a transference relationship begin.

Susan Isaacs and the Malting House School

Philip Graham

Philip Graham

Philip Graham  

Early years education, psychoanalysis, Susan Isaacs, history

Abstract

It is well known that psychoanalysis has over the years had a significant impact on the education of children with mental health problems. Its contribution to the theory and practice of mainstream education is less well documented. This paper gives an account of the five-year (1924–1929) history of the Malting House School in Cambridge. The school was financed by Geoffrey Pyke and headed by Susan Isaacs, a teacher, psychologist and early member of the British Psychoanalytic Society, who became a leading protagonist of the ideas of Melanie Klein. The physical structure, organisation, philosophy and curriculum of the school are described. Although the school was only in existence for five years, through the writings and teaching of Susan Isaacs it had a lasting impact on early years education.

[[RunningHead]]

The use of board games in child psychotherapy

Ayala Oren

Ayala Oren

Ayala Oren  

Psychodynamic psychotherapy, game play, board games, emotional development

Abstract

Playing checkers, football or more recently, computer games, is an important part of the latency child's culture. The ability to play games demands a level of emotional development similar to that needed to cope with the emotional/developmental demands characteristic of latency. A game shared by the therapist and child provides a picture of the child's development, patterns of interaction and internalised representations, and is an arena where the therapist can intervene, verbally and non-verbally, in response to the specific needs of the child. The child's desire and need to play clash with the difficulties in coping with the demands of the game. This raises the same issues that children confront during their maturation and interactions with others. Observation and analysis of game play allow the skilled therapist to evaluate the emotional development, internal representations, projections and patterns of relations of children and to intervene to help them with their specific difficulties and conflicts and, importantly, do so in an enjoyable way. The special challenges for the therapist using board games in psychotherapy come from the need simultaneously to observe the game, play it ‘well’, plan actions, regulate the child's anxiety level, maintain a playing atmosphere and deal with transference and countertransference issues – all in the highly tense atmosphere of competition. In the paper, I outline how board games can be used in psychotherapy, focusing on projective and developmental domains. I present a scheme that links emotional development stages and their expressions in game play, and use a case description to illustrate how it can be used in assessment, treatment planning and following progress. Some of the dilemmas faced by the therapist using games in therapy are also discussed.

The development of work discussion groups in educational settings

Emil Jackson

Emil Jackson

Emil Jackson  

Teacher support groups, consultation, continuing professional development, secondary school, staff training

Abstract

This paper describes the application and development of the work discussion method within educational settings. In the first section of the paper, I outline some key contextual factors that are important to consider when setting up work discussion groups within schools. A number of case examples are then described, illustrating a range of central issues that can emerge. By developing a deeper understanding about the meaning of behaviour and the emotional factors that impact on teaching and learning, I hope to demonstrate how work discussion groups can help teachers to develop their capacity to manage the challenges of their work, role and relationships with pupils. More broadly, I hope to illustrate how these groups can help to promote a learning environment for all, in which development and growth is promoted at a personal, professional and whole school level.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

This is another general edition of the Journal, which reflects in particular the international character of debate and exchange within our profession, with articles by authors from the UK, the USA and the Middle East, as well as a Clinical Commentary contribution from Australia. All the articles in this edition in one way or another have as a central theme issues of technique or the application of child psychotherapy in different settings.

We were delighted to award the clinical essay prize to Kate Robertson for her paper ‘Pussy Cat, Pussy Cat, Where have you been?’ An account of intensive psychotherapy with a seven‐year-old boy in a special school’. The paper was originally presented at the 2007 ACP Annual Conference. Robertson's paper vividly shows the experience of setting up and carrying out intensive psychotherapy in a special school setting, which in this case was very well supported by the school. From the outset, therapy was offered for one year and the paper traces the several mini-endings during the breaks between sessions as well as addressing the child's reluctant accommodation to the final ending. Although working with a markedly disabled and delayed child was not the main topic of the paper, the establishment between child and therapist of a proto- and then developed conversation/relationship (from banging to words with a differentiated other) offers a deeply intriguing account.

In this edition of the Journal, there are two articles on working with families or pairs of members within a family. In ‘Tripartite therapy with older children: mutuality in the relationship of a parent–child attachment’, the author, Nancy Berlin, provides a helpful map of some of the key ideas in attachment theory since Bowlby. The attachment perspective, as pioneered by Bowlby and significantly expanded upon by Ainsworth and Main, has for a long time been of interest to child psychotherapists who, from their own framework(s), know the need for a secure base provided by the primary caregiver and are also familiar with some of the literature. Of especial interest to our readership will be seeing how these insights are applied and worked within a clinical context. ‘Tripartite psychotherapy’ is defined as ‘a technique of psychoanalytic psychotherapy of the parent–child relationship with both parent and child in the room together with the therapist. It is a flexible, psychoanalytically oriented approach to parent–child relationship problems, particularly useful when the primary attachment has gone awry’. Berlin argues that the case of Emma, a 12‐year-old adopted girl with a longstanding embattled relationship with her adopted mother, is best addressed with the two of them in the room rather than the girl being offered individual help and the themes of abandonment, rejection and her frustrated needs for intimacy being taken up in a transference relationship.

‘Who owns my pain?’ An aspect of the complexity of working with looked after children

Marigemma Rocco-Briggs

Marigemma Rocco-Briggs

Marigemma Rocco-Briggs  

CAMHS, foster carers, network, fostering, consultation, deprivation, abuse, acting out, social workers, psychotherapeutic understanding

Abstract

This paper underlines the difficulties of working with looked after children and their carers. The author discusses a particular approach to respond to the complexity of looked after children's emotional difficulties, and their impact on the network of professionals making decisions about their life in care. As their own parents are no longer in a position to take responsibility for them, their trauma and past abuse make for a lack of clarity amongst this network when establishing the responsible role in loco parentis. In order to provide effective therapeutic work with these children, it is crucial to consider their disturbance as affecting the network around them. Enabling the network to understand and process powerful feelings around the child enhances its self-reflective function, so crucial for thinking about the child's needs and emotional development.

From scapegoating to thinking and finding a home: delivering therapeutic work in schools

Graham Music and Becky Hall

Becky Hall

Becky Hall  

Schools, child psychotherapy, splitting, scapegoat, labelling

Abstract

This paper discusses how the child psychotherapist's core skills can be usefully applied in a school setting. It outlines some of the important policy changes that have necessitated a move towards delivering therapeutic work in community settings such as schools. It is argued that the role of the child psychotherapist in schools has much in common with the role played by the psychotherapist in a therapeutic community. The paper suggests that therapy in schools is in many ways less simple than therapy in clinic settings, and in particular it is often unclear who exactly the client is and at what level to intervene when a referral is made. The referred patient is not necessarily the ‘problem’, so that the child psychotherapist must be prepared to tackle issues in the system to ensure that splitting and projection are reduced, and systems around children can become more containing. Clinical vignettes and one main clinical illustration are used to try to illustrate these points.

Workers, groups and gangs: consultation to residential adolescent teams

Simon Cregeen

Simon Cregeen

Simon Cregeen  

Consultation, adolescents, looked after children, residential units, team dynamics, groups and gangs

Abstract

This paper discusses how the internal worlds of adolescents who are looked after in residential care homes impact upon workers and generate complex dynamics within teams. This is especially so regarding internal parental objects and couplings, which inevitably include those of abandoning, abusive and ambivalent parental figures. Versions of these are projected and enacted between adolescents and workers, workers and managers, team and consultant. Conceptual thinking about groups and gangs is drawn upon to help illuminate the emotional phenomena encountered in team consultation meetings as described in the paper. Clinical material is given of working in the transference as consultant to the team, in order to illustrate processes of containment and the opportunity for thinking to take place. In this, there is movement between different states of mind within the team. The paper seeks to demonstrate a way of consulting to residential teams working with looked after adolescents and to show how this can mediate some of the enactments by workers and teams of projected states and transferential phenomena. Associated with this, there can be a deepening of the team's understanding of the emotional experience of the adolescents in their care.
